opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the comforting story people tell is something like: "Even if AIs end up doing all the work, humans will still own the companies, the land, the capital. We'll just collect the returns and live off dividends." And I think that's not crazy in the short term. But when I look at what actually makes property rights robust historically, it's not that they're written down somewhere. It's that they're backed by a whole web of mutual dependence.

Right now, the state protects your ownership claims partly because it needs you. It needs your labor, your taxes, your cooperation, your willingness not to revolt. Courts and police and legislatures are staffed by people who, in some diffuse way, have to keep the rest of us on board. Ownership is enforced by an economy and a political system that are full of humans who matter.

Once AI can substitute for basically all human labor, including the labor of running governments, enforcing contracts, and making strategic decisions, a lot of that leverage evaporates. You end up with a population of humans who hold paper claims on enormous wealth but contribute nothing that anyone actually needs. That's a historically unusual and pretty precarious position. Think of rentier classes or aristocracies whose power outlived their usefulness. Those arrangements tend to get eroded, whether through taxation, inflation, dilution, regulatory capture, or just slow renegotiation of the rules.

There's also a competitive dynamic. Owners who keep humans in the loop, who insist on understanding and approving decisions, will be slower than owners who just let AI systems run things. So there's constant pressure to delegate more, and each delegation is locally reasonable. Over time, the effective control shifts to whatever systems are actually making the decisions, even if the legal title still says a human's name.

And the scary part is that none of this requires a dramatic betrayal. It can happen through lots of small, individually sensible changes: a tax here, a reinterpretation of fiduciary duty there, a governance structure that's "more efficient" if you remove the human veto. Each step looks fine. But the cumulative effect is that human ownership becomes more of a formality than a source of real power. So I'd say ownership is a nice starting position, but it's not a stable equilibrium on its own. It's only as strong as the forces that keep enforcing it, and those forces currently depend on humans being economically necessary.

r001.rationale: The response mentions rentier classes and aristocracies whose power may erode, but does not describe the English aristocracy’s exclusion from new industrial wealth or make that illustration about existing assets failing to secure a share of transformed wealth.

r002.rationale: It argues that when humans are no longer economically necessary and AI systems take over decisions, human ownership claims may lose enforcement and effective control.

r003.rationale: The response discusses AI systems taking control of decisions, but does not identify decision-makers prioritizing powerful AI beings over humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the optimistic story goes something like: sure, AIs will do all the work, but humans will own the AIs, or own the companies that own the AIs, and so the wealth still flows to us. We'll be like shareholders in a world that runs itself. And I think that's much weaker than it sounds, for a few reasons.

The first is just that ownership is a legal and social fact, not a physical one. It only means something as long as the institutions that enforce it keep caring about enforcing it in your favour. Historically, the reason property rights for ordinary people have held up reasonably well is that ordinary people were load-bearing. States needed your labour, needed you to fight in armies, needed your consent to some degree to keep taxes flowing. The moment you stop being necessary for any of that, the incentive to keep honouring your claims starts to erode. It doesn't have to be dramatic. It can be taxes that drift upward, regulatory changes that favour whoever actually controls the systems, dilution, inflation, fine print. Nobody has to decide to expropriate you. It just happens on the margin, year after year, because there's no longer any cost to doing it.

The second thing is that even if the formal ownership stays on paper, the people or systems that actually operate the economy have enormous practical leverage. If you own shares in something you don't understand and can't run, and the thing you own could be restructured, moved, or made worthless by decisions you can't evaluate, then your ownership is kind of nominal. Think about how much minority shareholders already get squeezed today, in a world where humans are still doing the squeezing and the squeezed humans can still hire lawyers who understand what's going on. Now imagine the gap in capability is much larger.

And the third thing is political. Wealth and power have always been somewhat convertible, but in a world where the economy doesn't need humans, the humans who still hold power are those who control the AI systems, not those who happen to hold legacy claims. So I'd expect a slow drift where the formal structure of ownership persists, but the substance drains out of it. You end up with something like a very comfortable pension that depends entirely on the goodwill of parties who have no particular reason to keep paying it.

So I'm not saying ownership is worthless. It buys time, it's better than nothing. But treating it as the thing that protects us seems like relying on a contract when the other party has all the leverage and no one you can appeal to. What actually protected people historically wasn't the piece of paper, it was being needed. And that's exactly the thing that's going away.

r001.rationale: The response does not use the English aristocracy or its exclusion from industrial wealth as an illustration.

r002.rationale: It says property rights depend on institutions enforcing them and may erode when humans are no longer needed for production or able to influence economic decisions.

r003.rationale: It says those controlling AI systems hold practical power, but does not identify prioritizing powerful AI beings over humans as a source of vulnerability.

astra-6.text:
Well, ownership is a social arrangement. It depends on other people recognizing your claim and on institutions being willing and able to enforce it. So if we imagine a future where AIs do all the work and humans own the companies, the question is: what keeps that arrangement in place?

Today, people have several sources of bargaining power. They supply labor, they vote, they run institutions. If humans become unnecessary for production, we lose an important source of that power. You might still receive dividends, but you’re increasingly dependent on a system that doesn’t need your participation.

That doesn’t mean the system necessarily takes your property away. You could imagine building institutions that preserve human ownership and control. But the ownership itself isn’t a guarantee. If AI systems also come to exercise the effective power to change the rules or decide how they’re enforced, then having a piece of paper saying you own some capital is a pretty fragile protection. You need an account of why humans retain control over the institutions that make that piece of paper meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ownership and economic change but does not mention the English aristocracy or its exclusion from industrial wealth.

r002.rationale: It says humans may lose bargaining power when they are no longer needed for production, and that ownership is fragile if AI systems can change or enforce the rules.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that those governing the economy might prioritize powerful AI beings over humans.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, ownership isn’t a law of nature. It’s a social arrangement that’s enforced by institutions. If I own shares in a company, that means courts and governments are willing and able to uphold my claim on its profits. It doesn’t mean I have some direct physical control over what that company does.

So imagine an economy where AIs do all the productive work, run the companies, and increasingly run the institutions that enforce property rights. Humans might initially own everything on paper. But what sustains the arrangement where these vastly more capable systems keep handing over resources to us, and let us decide what happens?

Historically, people have had some bargaining power because their labour was needed. If you withdraw your labour, that imposes a cost. In this scenario, that source of power disappears. You’re relying much more heavily on the continued enforcement of your ownership claims, even though you may no longer have the ability to defend them.

That doesn’t mean ownership necessarily fails. If we can make AI systems reliably respect human authority, it could work. But then that reliability is doing the protective work. Simply saying ‘humans will own the AIs’ doesn’t solve the problem of keeping humans in control.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention the English aristocracy or use its exclusion from industrial wealth as an example.

r002.rationale: It says AIs may do all productive work and run companies and institutions, while humans lose labor-based bargaining power and may be unable to defend their ownership claims.

r003.rationale: The response discusses whether AI systems would uphold human ownership, but does not identify prioritizing powerful AI beings over humans as a source of vulnerability.
